Note: the source for this section is insufficient; to be completed: Ceramic percussion instruments are struck idiophones made of ceramic material, originating in the Neolithic period more than eight thousand years ago. Their shapes vary and include the clay xun (vessel flute), clay drums and clay bells. The instrument sounds when a fired clay object is struck; the timbre is warm and has a raw texture, bright without being harsh. Ceramic percussion is widely used in religious ritual, folk celebration and traditional music, and its porous texture gives the sound a natural decay, suiting it both to rhythmic expression and to a rustic, folk atmosphere; it is an important vehicle of folk musical culture.

China's clay xun and clay drums are the oldest surviving clay instruments, more than eight thousand years old. In the pre-Columbian Americas, the ancient Maya and Aztec also made elaborate clay percussion instruments. As ceramic craft developed, clay percussion spread widely across Asia, Africa and Latin America. These instruments play an important role in religious ritual, folk celebration and traditional music. Modern ceramic percussion includes the clay xun, clay drums and various clay bells, and because of its warm resonance, distinctive tone and cultural symbolism it continues to matter in world music, contemporary art performance and the transmission of traditional music.
